en: Thus have I heard: [The Discourse on Corruptions, Majjhima Nikāya 128].
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, the monks at Kosambī were living in strife, quarreling, and engaged in disputes, stabbing one another with verbal daggers.
Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here in Kosambī the bhikkhus have taken to quarreling, brawling, and falling into disputes; they dwell stabbing one another with the weapons of the tongue.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach those bhikkhus out of compassion.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to them:
“Enough, bhikkhus! Do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not contend, do not argue.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One come, venerable sir;
the Blessed One is the Lord of Dhamma.
May the Blessed One, venerable sir, dwell at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life.”
“We shall be known by this quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute.
A second time, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, bhikkhus! No more quarreling, no more strife, no more contention, no more dispute.”
A second time, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One wait, O Lord;
the Blessed One is the Master of the Dhamma."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One dwell at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life;
we shall be known by this quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute.
A third time, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, bhikkhus; do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not argue, do not contend.
For a third time, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One wait, venerable sir.”
“The Blessed One is the Lord of Dhamma;
let the Blessed One, venerable sir, dwell at ease, devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life.
We shall be known by this quarrel, dispute, contention, and strife.”
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kosambī and returned from his almsround after the meal, he put away his lodging, took his bowl and robe, and while still standing, uttered these verses:
“The crowd is loud, the people are clamorous;”
When the Saṅgha was being split, no one thought,
"I am a fool," nor did they think anything else more than that.
Those who appear wise but are utterly deluded,
speaking only within the range of mere words,
will stretch their mouths as far as they desire.
The wise do not understand that by which they are led:
"He abused me, he struck me,
he defeated me, he robbed me."
And those who harbor resentment toward such a person,
their enmity is not appeased.
"He abused me, he struck me," [they think].
"He has conquered me, he has defeated me";
yet for those who do not harbor resentment toward him,
their enmity is stilled.
For enmities are never appeased in this world by enmity;
they are appeased only by non-enmity.
This is the eternal Dhamma.
Others do not understand it,
yet we here strive for it.
And those who understand this therein,
their quarrels are thereby stilled—
those who break the bones and take away life.
Even for those who seize the wealth of cattle and plunder the kingdom,
there still exists a meeting together.
Why should it not be so for you?
If one should find a wise companion,
a steadfast friend who walks with one and dwells in virtue;
Having overcome all dangers,
one should wander with a mind at ease and mindful.
If one does not find a wise companion, [one should wander alone].
Walking together with one who is steadfast and dwells in goodness,
one should eventually leave them behind— just as a king leaves a conquered kingdom—
and wander alone like a tusker elephant in the forest.
Wandering alone is better;
there is no companionship with a fool.
One should wander alone and commit no evil deeds.
“Free from anxiety, like an elephant in the Mātanga forest.
Then the Blessed One, having spoken these verses while still standing, approached the village of Bālakaloṇakāra.
Now at that time, the Venerable Bhagu was dwelling in the village of Bālakaloṇakāra.
The Venerable Bhagu saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, he prepared a seat and water for washing the feet.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, he washed his feet.
The Venerable Bhagu, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Bhagu was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it bearable, monk? Is it sustainable? Are you not distressed by lack of almsfood?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is sustainable, Blessed One; and I am not distressed by lack of almsfood, Bhante.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Bhagu with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and went to the Eastern Bamboo Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila were dwelling in the Eastern Bamboo Grove.
The grove-keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar,
and having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Do not enter this park, Great Ascetic.
There dwell three sons of good family who live intent upon their own welfare.
Do not cause them discomfort.”
The Venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper as he was conversing with the Blessed One.
Having heard this, he said to the park keeper:
"Friend park keeper, do not prevent the Blessed One."
“The Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila; having approached them, he said to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila:
“Come forward, venerable sirs, come forward! The Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila went out to meet the Blessed One;
one received the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, he washed his feet.
Those three venerable ones, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the venerable Anuruddha was sitting there to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“I hope it is bearable for you, Anuruddhas; I hope it is livable; I hope you are not troubled by lack of almsfood?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One; and we are not troubled by lack of almsfood, Bhante.
“But I hope that you, Anuruddhas, dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of love?”
“Indeed, Bhante, we live in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of love.
“But how, Anuruddhas, do you live in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of love?
“In this regard, Bhante, it occurs to me thus:”
“It is indeed a gain for me, it is truly well-gained by me,
that I dwell together with such fellow-practitioners.
Venerable sir, toward these venerable ones, I maintain bodily acts of loving-kindness both openly and in private.
“Benevolent verbal action is maintained both openly and in private,
and benevolent mental action is maintained both openly and in private.
Regarding this, venerable sir, it occurs to me:”
‘What if I were to set aside my own mind and conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones?
Venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones.
For our bodies, venerable sir, are indeed diverse, but our minds, I think, are one.”
The Venerable Nandiya...
[and] the Venerable Kimila also said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it occurs to me as well:..."
"It is indeed a gain for me, it is truly well-gained by me,
that I dwell together with such fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
Venerable sir, toward these venerable ones, I maintain an attitude of loving-kindness through bodily action, both openly and in private.
“Benevolent verbal action is established both openly and in private,
and benevolent mental action is established both openly and in private.
Regarding this, venerable sir, it occurs to me:”
‘What if I were to set aside my own mind and conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones?
Venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones.
For indeed, venerable sir, our bodies are diverse, but we seem to have but one mind.”
“In this way, Bhante, we dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, looking upon one another with eyes of love.
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!
But do you, Anuruddhas, dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?”
“Indeed, Bhante, we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“But in what way, Anuruddhas, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?
“Here, Bhante, whichever among us returns first from the village with almsfood prepares the seats, sets out water for drinking and water for washing, and places a refuse bucket.

When one returns from the village after the alms round—if there is food left over from the meal and he desires it, he eats it; if he does not desire it, he discards it where there is little vegetation or throws it into water that contains no living beings.
He puts away the seats; he puts away the drinking water and the washing water; having washed the refuse bowl, he puts it away; he sweeps the dining hall.
Whoever sees that the water jar for drinking, the water jar for washing, or the chamber pot is empty and void, he refills it.

“If there is something for us that is beyond our capacity, we call to a second person with a gesture of the hand and have it brought by passing it from hand to hand; yet, venerable sir, we do not break our word on that account.
Furthermore, venerable sir, every five days we sit together all night long in discussion on the Dhamma.
It is in this way, venerable sir, that we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddhas!
But while you are dwelling thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?
“In this regard, venerable sir, while we are dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, we perceive a radiance and a vision of forms.”
"But that radiance and the vision of forms disappeared before long,
and we did not penetrate that sign. "Anuruddhas, you must indeed penetrate that sign."
"Anuruddha, formerly, before my enlightenment while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, I perceived light and saw forms.
But after a short time, that light of mine vanished and the vision of forms disappeared.
Then, Anuruddha, this thought occurred to me:"
“What now could be the cause, what the condition, why this radiance has vanished from me and my vision of forms?
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
“Doubt has arisen in me, and because of that doubt, my concentration has lapsed.”
“When concentration has lapsed, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear.
I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again.
Then, Anuruddha, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived both the radiance and the vision of forms.
Then, before long, that radiance of mine vanished, as did my sight of forms.
It occurred to me, Anuruddha:
“What is the cause, what is the condition, for this radiance of mine to vanish and my sight of forms to cease?”
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
"Non-attention has arisen in me, and because of that non-attention, my concentration has lapsed.
When concentration has lapsed, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear."
"I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again, nor will there be lack of attention.
Then, Anuruddha, ...
[as before] ... it occurred to me, Anuruddha:
“Dullness and drowsiness have arisen in me, and because of dullness and drowsiness, my concentration has lapsed.
When concentration has lapsed, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear.
I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor dullness and drowsiness.”
Thus, Anuruddhas, ...
[as before] ... it occurred to me, Anuruddhas:
"Terror arose within me, and because of that terror, my concentration lapsed."
When concentration was lost, the radiance and the vision of forms vanished.
Just as if, Anuruddha, a man traveling along a road were to have two snakes spring up on both sides of him and he would experience terror because of that;
even so, Anuruddha, terror arose within me, and because of that terror, my concentration lapsed.
"When concentration has lapsed, the illumination and the vision of forms disappear.
Therefore, I shall act in such a way that neither doubt, nor lack of attention, nor sloth and torpor, nor trepidation will arise in me again.
Thus, Anuruddha, ...pe...
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
"Exhilaration has arisen in me, and because of that exhilaration, my concentration has lapsed.
When concentration lapses, the radiance disappears, as do the vision of forms."
"Just as if, Anuruddha, a man searching for one entrance to a treasure were suddenly to find five entrances to treasures, and because of that a thrill would arise in him;
even so, Anuruddha, a thrill arose in me, and through that thrill my concentration lapsed.
When concentration had lapsed, the radiance vanished and the vision of forms disappeared."
"I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again, nor lack of attention, nor sloth and torpor, nor trepidation, nor elation.
Then, Anuruddhas, ...
[as before] ... it occurred to me, Anuruddhas:
“Coarseness has arisen in me, and because of this coarse legal issue, my concentration has lapsed.
When concentration lapses, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear.
I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again, nor inattention, nor sloth-and-torpor, nor trepidation, nor elation, nor coarseness.”
Thus, Anuruddha, ...
[as before] ... it occurred to me, Anuruddha:
"Excessive energy has arisen in me, and because of this excessive energy, my concentration has lapsed."
"When concentration has lapsed, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear.
Just as if, Anuruddha, a man were to grasp a quail tightly with both hands, it would die right then and there;
even so, Anuruddha, excessive energy arose in me, and because of that excessive energy, my concentration lapsed."
"When concentration has lapsed, the illumination and the vision of forms disappear.
Therefore, I shall act in such a way that neither doubt, nor lack of attention, nor sloth and torpor, nor trepidation, nor elation, nor grossness, nor over-exertion of energy will arise in me again.
Thus, Anuruddha, ...pe...
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
"An excessively slackened energy has arisen in me; and because of that excessive slackening of energy, my concentration has lapsed.
When concentration lapses, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear."
"Just as if, Anuruddha, a man were to catch a sparrow loosely and it would fly up from his hand;
even so, Anuruddha, excessive laxity of energy arose in me, and because of that excessive laxity of energy, my concentration fell away.
When concentration had fallen away, the radiance disappeared and the vision of forms vanished."
"I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again, nor lack of attention,
nor sloth and torpor, nor trepidation, nor elation, nor grossness, nor over-exerted energy,
nor overly slackened energy."
Thus, Anuruddha, ...
[as before] ... it occurred to me:
“A longing has arisen in me, and because of that longing, my concentration has lapsed.”
When concentration has lapsed, the illumination and the vision of forms disappear.
I shall act in such a way that neither doubt, nor lack of attention, nor sloth and torpor, nor nervousness, nor elation, nor bodily rigidity, nor over-exertion of energy will arise in me again.
‘Neither with overly slackened energy nor with longing.
Then, Anuruddhas, as I was dwelling thus … [as before] … it occurred to me, Anuruddhas:
‘The perception of diversity arose in me, and because of that perception of diversity, my concentration fell away.
When concentration had fallen away, the radiance and the vision of forms disappeared.
Therefore, I shall act in such a way that neither doubt nor lack of attention will arise in me again.’
“Lassitude and drowsiness, trepidation, elation, levity, over-exertion of energy,
slackness of energy, longing, and perceptions of diversity.
Anuruddha, dwelling thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived both light and the vision of forms.
Then, before long, that radiance of mine vanished, as did the sight of forms.
It occurred to me, Anuruddha:
"What is the cause, what is the condition, why this radiance of mine has vanished and the sight of forms?"
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
"Excessive brooding over forms has arisen in me; and because of that excessive brooding over forms, my concentration has lapsed.
When concentration lapses, the radiance and the vision of forms disappear."
"I shall act in such a way that doubt will not arise in me again,
nor lack of attention, nor sloth and torpor, nor trepidation, nor elation, nor grossness, nor over-exertion of energy,
nor slackness of energy, nor longing, nor perceptions of diversity, nor excessive preoccupation with forms."
Thus, Anuruddha, having understood: "Doubt is a defilement of the mind," I abandoned doubt as a defilement of the mind;
having understood: "Inattention is a defilement of the mind," I abandoned inattention as a defilement of the mind;
having understood: "Lethargy and drowsiness are a defilement of the mind," I abandoned lethargy and drowsiness as a defilement of the mind.
‘Trembling is an imperfection of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned trembling as an imperfection of the mind;
‘Agitation is an imperfection of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned agitation as an imperfection of the mind;
‘Coarseness is an imperfection of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned coarseness as an imperfection of the mind.
‘Excessive energy is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned excessive energy as a defilement of the mind;
‘Lax energy is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned lax energy as a defilement of the mind;
‘Longing is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned longing as a defilement of the mind.
‘Perception of diversity is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned perception of diversity as a defilement of the mind.
‘Excessive preoccupation with forms is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, I abandoned excessive preoccupation with forms as a defilement of the mind.
Then, Anuruddha, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived light but did not see forms.
“Indeed, Anuruddha, I saw forms but did not perceive light—
neither for the whole night, nor for the whole day, nor for the whole day and night.
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:”
‘What now could be the cause, what the condition, why I perceive light but do not see forms;
yet I see forms but do not perceive light—
for an entire night, for an entire day, and for an entire day and night?’
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
“When, having not brought to mind the sign of forms, I bring to mind the sign of light, at that time I perceive light but do not see forms.
But when, having not brought to mind the sign of light, I bring to mind the sign of forms, at that time I see forms but do not perceive light.”
"Whether for the whole night, or for the whole day, or for the whole day and night.
Anuruddha, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived a limited radiance and saw limited forms;
I perceived an immeasurable radiance and saw immeasurable forms.
‘Only for the entire night, or only for the entire day, or only for the entire day and night.
Then, Anuruddha, this occurred to me:
‘What is the cause, what is the reason, that I perceive only a limited radiance and see only limited forms?’”
“I perceive an immeasurable radiance and see immeasurable forms—
for an entire night, for an entire day, and for an entire day and night.
This thought occurred to me, Anuruddha:
‘On whatever occasion my concentration is limited, on that occasion my eye is limited.
With that limited eye, I perceive a limited radiance and see limited forms.
But on whatever occasion my concentration is immeasurable, on that occasion my eye is immeasurable.’
"Thus, with an immeasurable eye, I perceive an immeasurable radiance and see immeasurable forms—
the whole night, the whole day, and the whole day and night. When I understood, Anuruddhas,
"Doubt is a defilement of the mind," and having understood this, doubt as a defilement of the mind was abandoned by me.
‘Lack of attention is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, lack of attention as a defilement of the mind was abandoned;
‘Stiffness and torpor are a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, stiffness and torpor as a defilement of the mind were abandoned;
‘Trepidation is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, trepidation as a defilement of the mind was abandoned.
‘Excitement is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, excitement as a defilement of the mind was abandoned;
‘Coarseness is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, coarseness as a defilement of the mind was abandoned;
‘Over-exerted energy is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, over-exerted energy as a defilement of the mind was abandoned.
‘Excessive laxity of energy is a corruption of the mind’—having understood this, excessive laxity of energy as a corruption of the mind was abandoned;
‘Longing is a corruption of the mind’—having understood this, longing as a corruption of the mind was abandoned;
‘Perception of diversity is a corruption of the mind’—having understood this, perception of diversity as a corruption of the mind was abandoned.
‘Excessive brooding over forms is a defilement of the mind’—having understood this, excessive brooding over forms as a defilement of the mind was abandoned by me.
Then, Anuruddha, it occurred to me:
‘Those defilements of the mind that were mine have been abandoned.’
"Come now, I shall develop concentration in three ways.
And so, Anuruddha, I developed concentration with both applied thought and sustained thought; I developed concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only;
I developed concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought; and I developed concentration accompanied by rapture.

I cultivated concentration accompanied by rapture; I cultivated concentration free from rapture; I cultivated concentration accompanied by pleasure; I cultivated concentration accompanied by equanimity.

And so, Anuruddha, when concentration with directed thought and evaluation had been cultivated by me, and concentration without directed thought and with only evaluation had been cultivated, and concentration without directed thought and without evaluation had been cultivated, and concentration accompanied by rapture had been cultivated...
Concentration accompanied by rapture was developed; concentration free from rapture was developed; concentration accompanied by pleasure was developed;
concentration accompanied by equanimity was developed.
And knowledge and vision arose in me.
“Unshakable is my liberation of mind. This is my last birth; now there is no further becoming.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The venerable Anuruddha, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse on the Imperfections is finished; it is the eighth.
